title: Forces and one-dimensional deformation
prior_knowledge_summary: A force can change an object’s motion or shape.
Forces have direction and can act in opposite directions.
new_learning: Distinguish tensile and compressive forces in one dimension.
Use load, extension and compression to describe changes in length.

visual_planning.reason: Six distinct sketches support direction, measurement, comparison and synthesis without duplicating the same scene.
visual_planning.style: rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch

blocks.title: Why does the same object get longer or shorter?
content: Imagine a soft foam block between your hands. Pull its ends apart and it becomes longer. Push its ends together and it becomes shorter. The object is the same, but the directions of the forces are different.
Predict what happens to the length of a spring when equal forces pull outward at both ends, then when equal forces push inward.

figure.brief: Show one foam block in two panels: outward arrows and a longer block, then inward arrows and a shorter block. Keep labels to force direction and change in length.
figure.alt_text: Two panels show outward forces lengthening a block and inward forces shortening it.

blocks.title: Deformation is a change of shape or size
content: A force can deform an object. Deformation means that its shape or size changes. In this topic we study changes along one straight line.
The object may return to its original size later, or it may not. That question belongs to a later lesson. Here we focus on what the forces do and how the length changes.

figure.brief: Use a before-and-after ruler sketch of a wire with original length and changed length marked along one line.
figure.alt_text: A wire is shown before and after a one-dimensional change in length.

blocks.title: Tension pulls outward
content: When forces pull away from each other along an object, the object is under tension. These are tensile forces. They tend to make the object longer.
Think of a climbing rope supporting a climber. The climber pulls down on the rope while the support pulls up. The forces act away from the middle of the rope, so the rope is in tension.

figure.brief: Sketch a rope segment with equal outward arrows at its ends and a small enlarged view showing the segment lengthening.
figure.alt_text: A rope segment has outward arrows at both ends and becomes longer.

blocks.title: Compression pushes inward
content: When forces push toward each other along an object, the object is under compression. These are compressive forces. They tend to make the object shorter.
A chair leg supports a person. The seat pushes down on the leg and the floor pushes up. Both forces point toward the middle of the leg, so the leg is compressed.

figure.brief: Sketch a chair leg with inward arrows, then place a small tension sketch beside it with arrow directions highlighted in different colours.
figure.alt_text: A chair leg is compressed by inward forces beside a rope pulled by outward forces.

blocks.title: Reading load and change in length
content: Load is the force applied to an object. Suppose a wire has original length 0.800 m. A tensile load changes its length to 0.803 m.
Extension is the increase in length. Here extension = final length - original length = 0.803 m - 0.800 m = 0.003 m. The positive change matches the outward pull.
Now suppose a foam column has original length 0.120 m and a compressive load changes it to 0.116 m. The compression, meaning the decrease in length, is 0.120 m - 0.116 m = 0.004 m.
Check: each change is much smaller than the original length, which is sensible for the stated examples.

figure.brief: Create an annotated two-row layout showing original and final lengths for the wire and foam column, with subtraction aligned and units carried.
figure.alt_text: Original and final lengths are compared to find extension and compression.

blocks.title: Opposite forces do not mean no deformation
content: It is tempting to think that equal opposite forces cancel, so nothing happens. That idea is useful for motion of the whole object, but it does not tell us whether the object changes shape.

Equal outward forces can give zero resultant force while still stretching the object. Equal inward forces can give zero resultant force while still compressing it. Resultant force describes overall acceleration. Force direction at the ends helps us describe deformation.

figure.brief: Use a comparison table with columns overall motion and deformation for equal outward and equal inward forces.
figure.alt_text: A comparison shows that zero resultant force can coexist with stretching or compression.

blocks.title: A reliable three-step description
content: First, identify the directions of the forces at the ends. Second, decide whether they pull away from or push toward the object’s middle. Third, state the change in length using extension for an increase or compression for a decrease.
Do not use Hooke’s law yet. This lesson builds the language needed before a mathematical force-extension model is introduced.

misconceptions_addressed: zero resultant force means no deformation
skills_students_can_now_use: classify a one-dimensional load as tensile or compressive
calculate extension or compression from two lengths
explain deformation despite zero resultant force
next_lesson_can_assume: extension is an increase in length
compression is a decrease in length
